prompt: A switch learns nothing from a frame's ___ address; it learns from where the frame came from.
sw1's table was empty. After one ping from pc1 to the server it held 02:9e:43:3e:ca:ae on p4. Which frame taught it that?
hint: Whose address is it, and in which field?

choices.text: pc1's echo request, which was addressed to the server
choices.why: A destination teaches a switch nothing.

choices.text: A frame sent by the server
choices.why: Right. Its source MAC arrived on p4.

choices.text: An announcement from the router on p8
choices.why: r1 sent nothing during this ping.

choices.text: A static entry the lab typed
choices.why: The command listed dynamic entries, learnt ones.

prompt: sw1 reports ageing_time 30000, in hundredths of a second. After how many minutes without a frame from it is an entry forgotten?
A laptop learnt on p1 is unplugged and plugged into p3. When does sw1's table show it on p3?

choices.text: After 300 seconds, when the old entry ages out
choices.why: The old one is replaced sooner than that.

choices.text: As soon as it sends a frame from p3
choices.why: Right. Its source arrives on p3 and rewrites the entry.

choices.text: When an administrator clears the table
choices.why: Learning needs no administrator.

choices.text: When another machine sends a frame to it
choices.why: A destination teaches nothing.

prompt: pc3's MAC, 02:d9:6b:02:17:20, is not in sw1's table, though pc3 is cabled and up. A frame for that address arrives on p1. What does sw1 do with it?
hint: It cannot drop it and cannot pick a port.

choices.text: Drops it, since the address is unknown
choices.why: Dropping would lose frames for a machine that is there and has not spoken yet.

choices.text: Asks for the MAC with ARP
choices.why: ARP asks for a MAC given an IP; a switch does neither.

choices.text: Sends it out of every port except p1
choices.why: Right. It floods, and pc3 receives it with everybody else.

choices.text: Sends it to p3, the port with no entry
choices.why: Several ports have no entry; the switch has no way to choose.

prompt: While pc1 pinged the server twice and then 10.20.10.99 twice, how many frames did pc3's tcpdump catch?
hint: Only the unknown destination reached pc3.

prompt: pc3 caught the pings to 02:00:00:00:00:99 and none of the pings to the server. Why the difference?
hint: Which of the two destinations was in the table?

choices.text: The server's port was in the table
choices.why: Right. 02:00:00:00:00:99 was not, and an unknown destination goes everywhere.

choices.text: Pings to a missing host are broadcasts
choices.why: They were unicast frames to one made-up MAC.

choices.text: tcpdump on pc3 only started after the server pings
choices.why: It ran for eight seconds, covering both pairs.

choices.text: The server's replies were too small to capture
choices.why: Size has nothing to do with it; the frames never reached pc3's port.

prompt: After the pings to 02:00:00:00:00:99, sw1's table still had 2 entries and none for that address. Why was it never learnt?

choices.text: The table was full
choices.why: It held two entries.

choices.text: Made-up addresses are filtered
choices.why: The switch flooded the frames, so it did not filter them.

choices.text: No frame ever came from it
choices.why: Right. It appeared only as a destination.

choices.text: Its entry aged out at once
choices.why: Ageing removes an entry after 300 seconds, and there was none to remove.

prompt: Which of these frames does a switch send out of every port but the incoming one? Choose all that apply.
hint: Two are flooded, and one is not even forwarded.

choices.text: A frame to ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff
choices.why: Right. A broadcast is for everybody.

choices.text: A frame to a MAC learnt on another port
choices.why: It goes to that one port.

choices.text: A frame to a MAC that is not in its table
choices.why: Right. Unknown destinations are flooded.

choices.text: A frame to a MAC learnt on the port it came in by
choices.why: The destination is behind the same port, so the switch drops it.

prompt: A monitoring server receives a steady stream of reports and sends nothing for ten minutes at a stretch. Other machines on its switch start seeing those reports. Why?
hint: Compare ten minutes with the ageing time.

choices.text: The reports are broadcasts
choices.why: They are addressed to one server, and they reach others only while it is silent.

choices.text: The switch's table is full
choices.why: A full table is one cause of flooding, but nothing here filled it.

choices.text: Its cable is damaged
choices.why: A cable fault loses frames; it does not copy them elsewhere.

choices.text: Its entry ages out after five silent minutes
choices.why: Right. Then frames to it are flooded until it speaks.

prompt: Put the steps of CSMA/CD on a shared Ethernet in order.
items: Wait until the medium is quiet
Notice a signal that is not your own
Wait a random time and try again
trap: The wait is random so that the two senders do not collide again on the next attempt.

prompt: A switch has 24 ports with one device on each. How many collision domains is that?
pc1's card reports Duplex: Full, and its collsns counter is 0. Why are there no collisions?
hint: What is shared on a full-duplex link?

choices.text: The link is fast enough to avoid them
choices.why: Speed does not prevent collisions; sharing causes them.

choices.text: Each direction has its own path
choices.why: Right. With nothing shared, nothing collides.

choices.text: The switch retries collided frames itself
choices.why: The counter would still record collisions.

choices.text: Too little traffic was sent
choices.why: Hundreds of frames would not collide either.

prompt: One end of a switched link is set by hand to full duplex; the other is left to negotiate and falls back to half. What does the link look like?
hint: Each end believes something different about the cable.

choices.text: Down, with no light on either port
choices.why: Both ends agree there is a link; they disagree about using it.

choices.text: Normal, because the switch corrects it
choices.why: Nothing corrects a setting typed by hand.

choices.text: Up, slow, and counting collisions
choices.why: Right. The half end counts collisions, and the full end counts damaged frames.

choices.text: Flooding, because the table empties
choices.why: Duplex has nothing to do with the MAC table.

prompt: A link on which a device sends or receives, but not both at the same moment, is ___ duplex.
pc3 captured 'Request who-has 10.20.10.22 tell 10.20.10.21', sent by pc1 to ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff. Why did it reach pc3?

choices.text: pc3 has the address 10.20.10.22
choices.why: pc3 is 10.20.10.23, and it did not answer.

choices.text: A broadcast goes out of every port
choices.why: Right. The switch floods it to everybody in the domain.

choices.text: The switch's table was full
choices.why: It was a broadcast; a full table is not needed to explain it.

choices.text: pc3's port was locked
choices.why: A lock limits what pc3 sends, not what it receives.

prompt: While pc1 broadcast the same ARP question again, isp, on r1's other interface, captured 0 packets. Why?

choices.text: tcpdump on isp filtered out ARP
choices.why: Its filter was arp, so it was listening for exactly that.

choices.text: r1's firewall dropped it
choices.why: The firewall judges forwarded packets; a broadcast is never forwarded.

choices.text: A router ends the broadcast domain
choices.why: Right. r1 received the question and passed it to no other network.

choices.text: The switch kept it away from p8
choices.why: Every port of sw1, p8 included, received the broadcast.

prompt: Match each device to how it divides a network.

pairs.right: One collision domain and one broadcast domain
One collision domain per port, one broadcast domain

right_distractors: One broadcast domain per port, one collision domain

prompt: Two switches, each with six PCs, are cabled to two different interfaces of one router. How many broadcast domains is that?
Three thousand machines share one flat switched network, and every one of them is busy answering broadcasts it does not need. Which change reduces that load?
hint: Which device ends a broadcast domain?

choices.text: Faster switches with more ports
choices.why: A faster switch still floods every broadcast to every port.

choices.text: A longer ageing time on every switch in the building
choices.why: Ageing affects learnt entries; broadcasts are flooded whatever the table says.

choices.text: Smaller networks, with routers between
choices.why: Right. Each router interface ends a broadcast domain; lesson 19 does it with VLANs.

choices.text: Full duplex on every link
choices.why: That removes collisions; broadcasts still reach everybody.

prompt: p3 was locked with learning off, and the table had nothing for it. pc3's ping got 0 replies. Why?
hint: What does a locked port check?

choices.text: pc3's IP address was wrong for this network
choices.why: It is 10.20.10.23/24, and it worked a moment later unchanged.

choices.text: Its source MAC was not entered for p3
choices.why: Right. Once the static entry was added, the same ping worked.

choices.text: Locking a port takes its link down
choices.why: The port stayed up; only unknown sources were refused.

choices.text: The server refused pc3
choices.why: Nothing from pc3 got past p3 to reach the server.

prompt: After pc3 changed its own MAC to 02:00:00:00:00:66, the locked port refused it again. What does that run show about locking by address?

choices.text: It proves which person is plugged in to the port
choices.why: The address is set by the machine's own software.

choices.text: It ages out after five minutes
choices.why: Static entries do not age.

choices.text: It checks an address the machine itself chooses
choices.why: Right. It stops the unregistered, and refuses honest changes too.

choices.text: It works on IP addresses as well
choices.why: It read the source MAC; the IP did not change.

prompt: A device on one port sends frames from thousands of made-up source addresses, and the switch has no port security. What happens to the other machines' traffic?

choices.text: It is flooded to every port
choices.why: Right. Their entries cannot stay in a full table, so their frames go everywhere.

choices.text: The switch shuts down until it is restarted
choices.why: A full table makes a switch flood, not stop.

choices.text: It is routed through the router instead
choices.why: The router is not involved in traffic inside one network.

choices.text: Nothing; real entries are kept first
choices.why: Nothing marks an entry as real; the table takes what arrives.

prompt: Which of these protect a switched network from strangers plugging in? Choose all that apply.
hint: Three are defences; two change something else.

choices.text: Disabling ports with nothing behind them
choices.why: Right. A free socket stops being an open one.

choices.text: A longer ageing time
choices.why: It changes how long entries live, not who adds them.

choices.text: A limit on addresses per port
choices.why: Right. It also stops a flood of made-up addresses.

choices.text: IEEE 802.1X
choices.why: Right. The port opens only after the device proves who it is.

choices.text: Full duplex on every port
choices.why: That removes collisions; a stranger still plugs in.

prompt: The IEEE standard in which a port carries nothing but the authentication exchange until the device proves who it is, is IEEE 802.___.
sw1's table is empty and pc1 pings the server for the first time. Put what sw1 does in order.
items: Learn pc1's MAC on p1 from its ARP request
Flood that broadcast out of every other port
Learn the server's MAC on p4 from its reply
Send the reply out of p1 only
trap: Learning comes before forwarding for every frame: pc1 is in the table before its broadcast leaves, which is why the reply needs no flood.

prompt: A switch port accepts one address at most. A user plugs a small unmanaged switch into it and connects two laptops. What happens?
hint: The port counts source addresses, not cables.

choices.text: Both work, since the small switch has one MAC
choices.why: An unmanaged switch forwards the laptops' frames with their own sources.

choices.text: The first laptop heard is accepted, the second refused
choices.why: Right. Two sources arrive on a port allowed one.

choices.text: Neither works, as a switch behind a port is refused
choices.why: The port judges addresses; it cannot see a switch.

choices.text: Both work, but at half duplex
choices.why: Duplex is a setting of the link, not of the address limit.

prompt: Match each observation to its cause.

pairs.left: Frames for one machine reach every port
pairs.right: Its address is not in the table

pairs.left: A PC is refused after changing its MAC
pairs.right: Its port is locked to an address

pairs.left: An ARP question never appears beyond the router
pairs.right: The router ends the broadcast domain

pairs.left: Collisions rise on a switched link
pairs.right: The two ends disagree on duplex

right_distractors: The ageing time is too long
